Abstract
We study the martingale property and moment explosions of a signature volatility model, where the
volatility process of the log-price is given by a linear form of the signature of a time-extended Brownian
motion. Excluding trivial cases, we demonstrate that the price process is a true martingale if and only
if the order of the linear form is odd and a correlation parameter is negative. The proof involves a fine
analysis of the explosion time of a signature stochastic differential equation. This result is of key practical
relevance, as it highlights that, when used for approximation purposes, the linear combination of signature
elements must be taken of odd order to preserve the martingale property. Once martingality is established,
we also characterize the existence of higher moments of the price process in terms of a condition on a
correlation parameter.
1
Introduction
The martingale property and moment explosions of the asset price process are fundamental considerations
in stochastic volatility modeling, particularly due to their implications for derivative pricing and numerical
methods. The martingale property is a key criterion for assessing the validity of a stochastic volatility model,
as emphasized by Sepp and Rakhmonov (2023). In particular, strict local martingale models exhibit structural
deficiencies, such as the failure of put-call parity and deviations in the asymptotic behavior of implied volatility
wings (Jacquier and Keller-Ressel, 2018). Similarly, the existence of moments for the price process plays a
crucial role in both theoretical and computational aspects of option pricing. In particular, the existence of
finite moments is crucial for ensuring the numerical stability and convergence of Monte Carlo methods used
to compute derivative prices and their sensitivities. Moments also play a key role in the proof of asymptotic
formulae, allowing one to transition from large deviations of the price process to call price asymptotics, see for
instance (Friz et al., 2021, Section 4.2).
Both of these problems have been extensively studied in the literature, dating back to the works of Girsanov
(1960) and Novikov (1973). However, Novikov’s criterion is often not applicable to stochastic volatility models.
Sin (1998) observed for the first time that in certain stochastic volatility models—such as the Hull–White
model—the stock price can be a strict martingale for certain parameter values. In this context, Lions and
Musiela (2007) present general sufficient conditions for martingality and strict local martingality when the
volatility process follows a stochastic differential equation (SDE), and also address the problem of moment
existence. Subsequently, Mijatovi´c and Urusov (2012) provide a more general criterion for martingality in
SDE-based models, while Bernard, Cui, and McLeish (2017) extend this work to the general spot-volatility

Most of these works, however, focus on Markovian models where both the asset price and volatility processes are
solutions of SDEs. For example, Jourdain (2004) proposes a martingality criterion, along with integrability
conditions for prices in SABR-like models. Similarly, Andersen and Piterbarg (2007) address the moment
problem and provide sufficient martingality conditions for SABR-like and Heston-like models.
In contrast, results in non-Markovian settings tend to be less general and are often derived on a case-by-case
basis. For instance, in the case of volatility processes governed by stochastic Volterra equations, several results
have been derived. For the rough Bergomi model, Gassiat (2018) establishes conditions for both martingality
and non-martingality, as well as a sufficient condition for moment explosions.
Gerhold, Pachschw¨oll, and
Ruf (2024) propose an alternative approach to verifying higher-order moment explosions by examining the
integrability of the price supremum and apply this method to the rough Bergomi model. In the context of the
Volterra Heston model, Abi Jaber, Larsson, and Pulido (2019) establish conditions for the martingale property,
while Gerhold, Gerstenecker, and Pinter (2018) study the problem of moment explosions. In the class of socalled path-dependent volatility (PDV) models (Guyon and Lekeufack, 2023), Nutz and Riveros Valdevenito
(2024) analyze the martingale property in a two-factor PDV model. Additionally, Ruf (2015) provides a general
martingality criterion for stochastic exponentials defined as non-anticipative path-dependent functionals of
solutions to stochastic differential equations. Despite its generality, this result cannot be directly applied to
stochastic volatility models and requires a thorough analysis to verify the condition for each particular model.
Recently, signature-based models have gained popularity in non-Markovian modeling. Such models were first
studied by Arribas, Salvi, and Szpruch (2020) and further developed by Cuchiero, Gazzani, and Svaluto-Ferro
(2023); Cuchiero, Gazzani, M¨oller, and Svaluto-Ferro (2025), and Abi Jaber and G´erard. Their distinguishing
feature is that the volatility process is represented as a (possibly infinite) linear combination of signature
elements. These models can serve both for the approximation, see Cuchiero et al. (2023), and the exaxt representation, see Abi Jaber and G´erard, of a wide range of models, though in both cases, the linear combination
of signature elements must be truncated for practical use. As we will demonstrate, the truncation order plays
a crucial role in determining whether the price process is a true martingale. However, no results on either
martingality or moment explosions have been established for these models so far. The aim of this paper is to
fill this gap by providing necessary and sufficient conditions for the martingality of the price process and by
studying the finiteness of its moments in signature volatility models. We adopt the multiplicative framework
of Abi Jaber and G´erard; Cuchiero et al. (2025), in which the price process is given by a stochastic exponential,
making the question of martingality non-trivial.
The Markovian setting provides key insights into the martingality problem.
In particular, for truncated
exponential Ornstein-Uhlenbeck models with negative spot-volatility correlation, obtained by truncating the
power series expansion of the exponential, the price process is a martingale if and only if the truncation order
is odd. A similar pattern appears in polynomial volatility models, where volatility is expressed as a polynomial
function of a Brownian motion or an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, as in the Quintic model of Abi Jaber, Illand,
and Li (2023). These results can be established using techniques similar to those in Lions and Musiela (2007,
Theorem 2.4(i)). Since path signatures play an analogous role to polynomials on path space, we expect similar
characterizations to hold beyond the Markovian framework.

The standard technique for verifying the martingale property reduces to studying the explosion time of a
certain stochastic differential equation (SDE) following a change of probability measure. In our case, this

Outline.
Section 2 introduces the necessary definitions and key concepts related to tensor algebra and signatures. In Section 3, we present our main results concerning the martingality criterion and moment explosions
for the signature volatility model. Section 4 establishes two essential bounds on signature words, which are
extensively used in the subsequent proofs. The proofs of these bounds are postponed to Section 6. Section 5
demonstrates how the martingality problem can be reduced to the explosion problem of a signature SDE.
Sections 7 and 8 are dedicated to proving the martingality and strict local martingality criteria, respectively.
Finally, Section 9 contains the proof concerning moment explosions.

In the case where X is a Brownian motion, the signature S(X) is a random element of T((Rd)) and S(X)t
is the truncated signature at order N.
The signature of a path X is the sequence of its iterated integrals, which can be thought of as a non-commutative
extension of the Fourier transform. The truncated signature at level N is the projection of the signature onto
the truncated tensor algebra T N(Rd).
The path signature is a powerful tool in stochastic analysis, as it allows to capture the entire history of a
stochastic process. It has been used extensively in the literature on rough paths, see for example (Lyons and
C, 1994), (Gubinelli, 2004), (Friz and Victoir, 2010), and more recently in financial applications, see
for example (Gassiat, 2021), (Friz et al., 2021), (Bayer et al., 2021).
2.2
Signature of a Brownian motion
We consider the case where X is a Brownian motion in Rd. The path signature S(X) is a random element of
T((Rd)), and it is known that S(X)t can be expressed as a sequence of iterated integrals, which are Gaussian
processes. The truncated signature S(X)N t is the projection of S(X)t onto T N(Rd). In the case where N = 1,
S(X)1 t = X t, and in the case N = 2, S(X)2 t = X t ⊗ X t − 1 2! (X t )⊗2.
In the case where d = 1, the signature simplifies to the sequence (1, X t, X t ⊗ X t, ..., (X t )⊗N ), which is
a classical multiplicative process.
